exercises.title: Techniques 1 — facilitated or independent?
exercises.problemHtml:
Two families of elicitation techniques: facilitated techniques interact with stakeholders (mainly discovering business and user requirements); independent techniques are done by the analyst alone to discover information and functionality users may not be aware of. Classify.

Requirements

  • Answer every question in the answer panel, then press Submit.
  • All answers must be correct to get Accepted; the explanations appear after you submit.

exercises.title: Techniques 3 — interviews and workshops done well
exercises.problemHtml:
Interviews: establish rapport, stay in scope, prepare questions and straw-man models (people critique more easily than create), suggest ideas, listen actively and paraphrase. Workshops: ground rules, all roles filled (facilitator, scribe, timekeeper), an agenda, a parking lot, time-boxed topics, a small team of the right people (5–6).

Requirements

  • Answer every question in the answer panel, then press Submit.
  • All answers must be correct to get Accepted; the explanations appear after you submit.

exercises.title: Techniques 4 — observation, questionnaires and analysis traps
exercises.problemHtml:
Observation may be passive (watch without interfering; protocol analysis — the performer explains while working; ethnography — long-term) or active (you join the work). Questionnaires suffer from biases; use a representative sample, unbiased and unambiguous questions, and redundant questions to detect inconsistency. User interface analysis: do not assume the new system needs a function just because the old one had it. Document analysis: documents may be out of date.

Requirements

  • Answer every question in the answer panel, then press Submit.
  • All answers must be correct to get Accepted; the explanations appear after you submit.
